doc_description: 3M Company’s 2022 Form 10‑K (ticker: MMM) details operations across four segments and full-year results while highlighting distinctive 2022 actions and risks: completion of the Food Safety split‑off with Neogen (~$2.7B gain), the announced spin‑off of its Health Care business, a decision to exit PFAS manufacturing by end‑2025 (~$0.8B impairment), and extensive litigation including the Aearo/Combat Arms earplug Chapter 11 and PFAS matters, together with PwC’s unqualified audits, market risk disclosures, and comprehensive financial statements.

structure.title: Preface
structure.summary:
- Document type and period: 3M Company Annual Report on Form 10-K for the fiscal year ended December 31, 2022 (Commission File No. 1-3285).
- Company identifiers and listing details: Incorporated in Delaware (EIN 41-0417775); principal offices in St. Paul, Minnesota; common stock (MMM) listed on the NYSE and Chicago Stock Exchange and also traded on the SIX Swiss Exchange; multiple registered notes listed on the NYSE.
- Filing status and compliance: Well-known seasoned issuer; large accelerated filer; timely filer of required reports and Interactive Data Files; not a smaller reporting company, emerging growth company, or shell company.
- Market and share data: Aggregate market value of nonaffiliate voting stock and shares outstanding as of January 31, 2023 provided; proxy statement to be incorporated by reference for Part III items.
- Form 10-K summary and table of contents: Hyperlinked cross-references to full disclosures; outline of Parts I–IV and Items, including:
  - Part I: Business; Risk Factors; Unresolved Staff Comments; Properties; Legal Proceedings; Mine Safety Disclosures.
  - Part II: Market for common equity and related matters; MD&A (Overview, Results of Operations, Performance by Business Segment and Geography, Critical Accounting Estimates, New Accounting Pronouncements, Liquidity, Financial Instruments); Market Risk disclosures; Financial Statements; and Notes.
  - Part III: Directors and governance; Executive Compensation; Ownership; Related party transactions; Auditor fees (to be provided via proxy).
  - Part IV: Exhibits and schedules; Form 10-K Summary.
- Financial statements and notes index: Consolidated statements (Income, Comprehensive Income, Balance Sheet, Changes in Equity, Cash Flows) for 2022, 2021, 2020; Management’s Responsibility and Report on Internal Control Over Financial Reporting; Independent auditor’s report; Notes 1–19 covering significant accounting policies, revenue, acquisitions/divestitures, goodwill and intangibles, restructuring, supplemental disclosures, income taxes, marketable securities, debt, pensions/postretirement, derivatives, fair value, commitments/contingencies, leases, stock-based compensation, and segment/geographic information.
- Business overview (Part I, Item 1): 3M is a diversified global technology company operating in four segments—Safety and Industrial; Transportation and Electronics; Health Care; and Consumer. It emphasizes product development, manufacturing, and marketing competencies, and faces competition from other technology-oriented companies.
- Available information: SEC filings accessible via SEC website; 3M provides its SEC reports on its investor website.
- Segment management and strategic update: Operations managed in four reportable segments; in July 2022, 3M announced its intention to spin off the Health Care business into a separate public company (referenced to Note 3).

- Reportable segments: Four segments—Safety and Industrial; Transportation and Electronics; Health Care; Consumer—organized to leverage shared technologies and resources.

structure.title: Business
structure.heading: ITEM 1 Business
structure.start_phrase: 3M Company was incorporated in 1929 under the laws of the State of Delaware to continue operations begun in 1902.
structure.summary:
- Overview and availability: 3M Company (ticker: MMM), incorporated in Delaware, provides its SEC filings and other investor materials via the SEC website and its own investor site.
- Business profile: A diversified global technology manufacturer operating in four segments—Safety and Industrial; Transportation and Electronics; Health Care; and Consumer—competing across numerous technologically driven markets.
- Segment structure and offerings: Detailed mapping of divisions to each segment, representative products, services, and brands (e.g., 3M Cubitron II, VHB tapes, Diamond Grade reflective sheeting, Tegaderm dressings, Post-it, Scotch, Scotch-Brite, Filtrete, Command) and key market trends/opportunities (e.g., personal safety, grid modernization, semiconductor, wound care, biopharma filtration, home improvement).
- Health Care separation: Announcement (July 2022) of intent to spin off the Health Care business into a separate public company; Food Safety business divested in 2022.
- Distribution: Multi-channel global sales model including direct, e-commerce, and broad networks of wholesalers, retailers, distributors, and dealers.
- Human capital: Approximately 92,000 employees (37,000 U.S.; 55,000 international) with focus areas in health and safety, employee development and succession, diversity/equity/inclusion (including a CEO Inclusion Council and $50M community investment commitment through 2025), and competitive compensation/benefits with flexible, trust-based work policies.
- Raw materials and supply chain: 2022 characterized by global supply imbalances and inflation; mitigation through inventory management, supplier relationships, alternative sourcing, and price-risk management; continued raw material price inflation.
- Intellectual property: Broad global portfolio of trademarks, patents, and trade secrets that provide competitive advantage; no single patent or family is essential to the company or any segment.
- Regulatory and environmental compliance: Operations subject to extensive U.S. and international regulations (e.g., product liability, antitrust, IP, FDA/healthcare, anti-bribery, trade, tax); ongoing environmental stewardship, remediation where required, and significant capital spending for environmental projects ($317M in 2022; approximately $646M expected across 2023–2024).
- Executive leadership: Listing of executive officers as of February 8, 2023, including Chairman and CEO Michael F. Roman and other senior leaders across technology, strategy, HR, operations, finance, legal, and business group leadership.
- Forward-looking statements: Caution regarding projections and assumptions, with identified areas of uncertainty including macroeconomic and geopolitical conditions, COVID-19 and public health events, PFAS-related liabilities and discontinuation plans, ERP implementation, cybersecurity, supply costs and availability, M&A/divestitures, debt and capital markets, taxes, asset impairments, legal/regulatory matters, Health Care spin-off, and the Aearo Entities’ Chapter 11 proceedings.
- Risk factors (excerpted): Exposure to global economic and geopolitical risks (e.g., inflation, recession, interest rates, trade tensions, sanctions, currency volatility), direct impacts from the Russia-Ukraine conflict (sanctions, supply disruptions, energy costs, cyber risk), potential impacts from climate change and related regulations, and disruptions from unexpected events such as pandemics (COVID-19) affecting demand, supply chain, manufacturing, distribution, and overall financial performance.

structure.title: Risk Factors
structure.heading: ITEM 1A Risk Factors
structure.start_phrase: Provided below is a cautionary discussion of what we believe to be the most important risk factors applicable to the Company.
structure.summary:
The excerpt centers on 3M’s Item 1A Risk Factors, plus brief Item 1B and Item 2 disclosures. Key points:

- Macro, geopolitical, and public health risks: Global operations (≈60% revenue outside the U.S.) expose 3M to economic downturns, inflation, interest rates, FX volatility, trade tensions (notably U.S.–China), protectionism, sanctions/export controls, and the Russia–Ukraine conflict (including supply disruptions, energy costs, cyber risks, and demand impacts). Climate change and related regulations may affect resources, energy, demand, and community health. COVID-19 caused supply chain and manufacturing challenges, shifting demand (initial surge then decline in respirators), market volatility, and reputational exposure (e.g., counterfeiting/price gouging).

- Foreign exchange: Strengthening U.S. dollar can adversely affect sales and earnings given the company’s international revenue mix.

- Legal and regulatory risks:
  - PFAS liabilities: Increasing global regulation and litigation related to PFAS; cooperation with regulators; historic phase-out of PFOA/PFOS; 2022 decision to exit all PFAS manufacturing and discontinue PFAS use by end of 2025 (recorded ~$0.8B pre-tax charge) with execution, replacement, cost, litigation, and customer relationship risks. Ongoing lawsuits (including AFFF MDL) and potential for material future charges (e.g., prior $897M MN settlement).
  - Broader compliance: Exposure to product liability, antitrust, IP, EHS, FCPA/anti-bribery, export controls/sanctions, FDA/healthcare laws (False Claims Act, anti-kickback, Sunshine Act), tax, and privacy laws; potential fines, operational limits, litigation, insurance shortfalls, reputational harm, and IP disputes.

- Products and customer preferences: Competitive dynamics, pricing, inventory/order pattern shifts, changing designs and preferences, and disruptive technologies (AI, blockchain, analytics) can affect demand and margins. Growth depends on successful, timely innovation and market acceptance.

- Supply chain and inputs: Vulnerability to availability and cost of components, raw materials, energy, and labor; risks from shortages, climate impacts, disasters, conflicts, logistics issues, regulatory actions (e.g., permits), and site disruptions.

- Business/operational risks:
  - Cybersecurity/IT: Threats to IT systems (including third-party and cloud providers) amid an ongoing global ERP/business transformation; risks heightened by remote work; potential data compromise, operational disruption, legal/regulatory exposure, and costs; insurance may not fully cover.
  - Portfolio actions and restructuring: M&A, alliances, divestitures, and organizational changes carry integration/synergy, benefit realization, revenue loss, and indemnity/liability risks.
  - Execution risk: Productivity and transformation initiatives (including ERP) may underdeliver or disrupt service, sales, and brand.

- Financial/capital markets and tax:
  - Pension/postretirement plans: Market performance and discount rates affect funding and results.
  - Credit ratings: Downgrades could raise funding costs and constrain capital access (current ratings: Moody’s A1/stable; S&P A+/CreditWatch negative as of Dec 2022).
  - Tax: Potential adverse impacts from changing tax laws and global reforms (e.g., OECD BEPS).

- Aearo Entities Chapter 11: Wholly owned subsidiaries filed to establish a 3M-funded trust for Combat Arms Version 2 earplug and respirator/asbestos claims; risks include legal uncertainty, reputational effects, liquidity and cost impacts, timing, and outcome unpredictability.

- Planned spin-off of Health Care business: Intended tax-free separation subject to multiple conditions; risks of delay, non-completion, dis-synergies, costs, disruption, talent retention, stakeholder relationships, and potential adverse tax outcomes.

- Item 1B: Unresolved Staff Comments—None.

- Item 2: Properties—Headquarters and major labs in St. Paul, MN; 61 U.S. manufacturing facilities in 29 states; 83 international facilities in 28 countries; majority of properties owned and shared across segments.

structure.title: Unresolved Staff Comments
structure.heading: ITEM 1B Unresolved Staff Comments
structure.start_phrase: null.
structure.summary:
- Outlines risks arising from Aearo Technologies’ and related subsidiaries’ voluntary Chapter 11 filings to establish a company-funded trust for liabilities tied to Combat Arms Version 2 earplugs and respirator/asbestos products, including legal uncertainties, reputational and stakeholder relationship impacts, liquidity and earnings risks, unknown total funding obligations under 3M’s funding/indemnification agreement, costs and duration of the proceedings, and the ability to reach settlements and confirm a reorganization plan.
- Details risks related to the planned spin-off of the Health Care business into a separate public company intended to be tax-free, including dependence on regulatory and board approvals and tax rulings, potential delays or changes reducing expected benefits, higher-than-expected costs and dis-synergies, operational disruptions, management distraction, talent retention challenges, stakeholder relationship impacts, and the possibility the transaction is not tax-free, which could lead to significant tax liabilities and adverse effects on business, financials, cash flows, and stock price.
- States there are no unresolved SEC staff comments.
- Provides a property overview: headquarters and major labs in St. Paul, Minnesota; 61 U.S. manufacturing facilities across 29 states; 83 international manufacturing/converting facilities across 28 countries; most properties are owned, suitable, and often shared across business segments.

structure.heading: ITEM 2 Properties
structure.summary:
- Outlines risks tied to the voluntary Chapter 11 filings by 3M’s wholly owned Aearo Entities to establish a company-funded trust for Combat Arms Version 2 earplug and respirator/asbestos-related claims, including legal uncertainties, reputational and counterparty impacts, liquidity and earnings effects, costs and duration of the proceedings, and the ability to reach settlements and confirm a reorganization plan; notes 3M’s funding and indemnification obligations and the unpredictability of timing, outcome, and financial impact.
- Details risks related to the planned spin-off of 3M’s Health Care business announced July 26, 2022, including reliance on multiple conditions (board approval, Form 10 effectiveness, IRS ruling, tax opinion), potential delays or changes that could reduce expected benefits, possible higher-than-anticipated costs and dis-synergies, operational and talent-retention challenges during the pendency, relationship impacts with key stakeholders, and tax risks if the transaction is not tax-free—any of which could negatively affect performance and stock price.
- Notes there are no unresolved SEC staff comments (Item 1B).
- Describes company properties (Item 2): headquarters and research facilities in St. Paul, Minnesota; 61 U.S. manufacturing facilities in 29 states; 83 international facilities in 28 countries; majority-owned, suitable facilities often used across multiple segments.

structure.title: Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations
structure.heading: ITEM 7 Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations
structure.start_phrase: Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations (MD&A) is designed to provide a reader of 3M’s financial statements with a narrative from the perspective of management.
structure.summary:
- Scope and structure: This is Item 7 MD&A, intended to provide management’s narrative on financial condition and results. It comprises eight sections: Overview; Results of Operations; Performance by Business Segment; Performance by Geographic Area; Critical Accounting Estimates; New Accounting Pronouncements; Financial Condition and Liquidity; and Financial Instruments.
- Forward-looking statements: Alerts readers to risks and uncertainties; references Item 1 “Cautionary Note Concerning Factors That May Affect Future Results” and Item 1A risk factors. Points to an April 26, 2022 Form 8-K for additional 2021 and 2020 MD&A information.
- Company overview and 2022 reporting changes: 3M is a diversified global manufacturer. Effective Q1 2022, it changed (1) the measure used for segment operating performance (impacting disclosed segment operating income and disaggregated revenue) and (2) certain non-GAAP measures to adjust for special items. The document reflects these changes for all periods presented.
- Segments and definitions: 3M operates in four segments—Safety and Industrial; Transportation and Electronics; Health Care; and Consumer. EMEA denotes Europe, Middle East and Africa. “Organic sales change” excludes impacts from foreign currency and acquisitions/divestitures (measured separately for 12 months post-transaction).
- COVID-19 effects: Mixed demand impacts across businesses and supply chain disruptions; overall results were primarily affected by demand shifts and supply chain issues; future impact remains uncertain.
- 2022 significant items and special charges/gains: About $2.3 billion pre-tax in significant litigation costs, including approximately $1.3 billion related to Combat Arms Earplugs litigation and about $355 million for PFAS-related commitments at Zwijndrecht, Belgium. Completed the split-off of the Food Safety Division, generating a pre-tax gain of roughly $2.7 billion. Committed to exit PFAS manufacturing by end of 2025, resulting in a 2022 pre-tax impairment charge of about $0.8 billion.
- Cross-references: Further details in Notes 2, 15, 16, and 19 and in the non-GAAP “Certain amounts adjusted for special items” section.

structure.title: Overview
structure.heading: Overview
structure.start_phrase: 3M is a diversified global manufacturer, technology innovator and marketer of a wide variety of products and services.
structure.summary:
- Scope and structure: Management’s Discussion and Analysis (MD&A) outlines eight sections (Overview; Results of Operations; Performance by Business Segment; Performance by Geographic Area; Critical Accounting Estimates; New Accounting Pronouncements; Financial Condition and Liquidity; Financial Instruments) and includes forward-looking statement cautions and references to prior filings for 2021/2020.

- 2022 reporting changes: Updated segment performance metric (business segment operating income) and revisions to non-GAAP measures to include broader “special items,” notably expanded litigation-related costs.

- Business profile and definitions: 3M operates in four segments—Safety & Industrial; Transportation & Electronics; Health Care; Consumer—and emphasizes “organic sales change” as sales excluding FX and M&A/divestiture impacts.

- Macroeconomic and external factors:
  - COVID-19: Mixed demand effects and supply chain disruptions.
  - Belgium PFAS site (Zwijndrecht): Operational interruptions, regulatory oversight, and an infraction report; ongoing restart progress.
  - Russia-Ukraine: Suspension of Russian operations, plan to exit and asset impairment charges; potential raw material supply disruptions.

- Significant 2022 events and special items:
  - Litigation costs approx. $2.3B pre-tax (Combat Arms Earplugs ~ $1.3B; PFAS-related matters at Zwijndrecht ~$355M).
  - Split-off of Food Safety business with a ~$2.7B pre-tax gain.
  - Decision to exit PFAS manufacturing by end of 2025 with ~$0.8B impairment charge.
  - Russia exit charges and divestiture-related restructuring.
  - Reclassification/handling of significant litigation costs across Corporate and Safety & Industrial, including Aearo-related bankruptcy context.

- Financial performance highlights:
  - Operating margin 2022: 19.1% GAAP vs 20.8% adjusted; EPS diluted $10.18 GAAP vs $10.10 adjusted.
  - Bridges detail impacts from organic growth/productivity, raw material/logistics inflation, FX headwinds, litigation/divestiture/PFAS/Russia items, and tax rate changes.
  - Effective tax rate: 9.6% in 2022 (benefit from Food Safety split-off tax structure); adjusted tax rate 17.7%.
  - Share count changes modestly benefited 2022 EPS.

- Segment and geography performance:
  - 2022 net sales $34.2B (-3.2%); organic growth +1.2%; FX -3.9%; divestitures -0.5%.
  - Segment operating income declines across all four segments; Corporate & Unallocated benefited from divestiture gain.
  - Regional mix: Americas 53.8%, APAC 28.9%, EMEA 17.3%; 2022 organic growth positive in Americas, flat to slightly negative elsewhere; notable country trends (e.g., U.S. flat total sales with +1% organic; China -6% total; Japan -12% total with +2% organic).
  - Currency risk management via natural and financial hedges (12–36 month horizons).

- Results of operations and costs:
  - Cost of sales up to 56.2% of sales due to litigation costs, inflation in materials/logistics, productivity headwinds (including Belgium shutdown) and investments; partially offset by pricing.
  - SG&A up to 26.5% from litigation, PFAS exit, Russia exit, restructuring; partly offset by cost controls.
  - R&D at 5.4% (down as a percent); continued investment in innovation.
  - Gain on divestitures (-8.0% of sales) from Food Safety split-off.
  - Goodwill impairment (0.8% of sales) tied to PFAS exit in Advanced Materials (within Transportation & Electronics).
  - Ongoing ERP deployment affecting cost lines.

- Capital allocation and liquidity:
  - Share repurchases of $1.5B in 2022; $4.2B remaining under authorization; continued dividend growth (65th consecutive year).
  - Reference to raw materials sourcing and availability elsewhere in the filing.

- Pensions and postretirement:
  - Global plans ~96% funded; primary U.S. plan 97% funded; asset returns -17.4% in 2022; discount rate increased to 5.18%.
  - Expected 2023 contributions $100–$200M; no required U.S. cash contribution; 2023 expense expected to decrease by ~$30M.

- Non-GAAP framework:
  - Clear reconciliation intent and rationale for excluding special items (litigation, divestiture costs/gains, restructuring, Russia exit, PFAS manufacturing exit), with placement of these items across Corporate or segments as applicable.

structure.title: Results of Operations
structure.heading: Results of Operations
structure.start_phrase: Refer to the preceding “Overview” section and the “Performance by Business Segment” section later in MD&A for additional discussion of sales change.
structure.summary:
- Results of operations overview with emphasis on operating expenses as a percent of net sales for 2022 vs. 2021:
  - Cost of sales: 56.2% vs. 53.2% (+3.0 pts)
  - SG&A: 26.5% vs. 20.4% (+6.1 pts)
  - R&D: 5.4% vs. 5.6% (−0.2 pts)
  - Gain on business divestitures: (8.0%) in 2022 vs. none in 2021
  - Goodwill impairment: 0.8% in 2022 vs. none in 2021
  - Operating income margin: 19.1% vs. 20.8% (−1.7 pts)
- Ongoing global ERP deployment impacting cost of sales, SG&A, and R&D.
- Cost of sales increased due to:
  - Special item costs for PFAS-related litigation and actions at Zwijndrecht, Belgium
  - Higher raw materials and logistics costs
  - Manufacturing productivity headwinds, including Belgium shutdown/restart impacts
  - Investments in growth, productivity, and sustainability
  - Partially offset by selling price increases
- SG&A increased due to:
  - Significant litigation costs (notably ~$1.2 billion pre-tax charge in Q2 2022 for Combat Arms Earplugs)
  - Impairment costs tied to exiting PFAS manufacturing
  - Costs related to exiting Russia
  - Divestiture-related restructuring charges
  - Continued investment in growth initiatives
  - Partially offset by restructuring benefits and cost management
- R&D as a percent of sales decreased; continued investment across application development, product/manufacturing support, product and technology development.
- Gain on business divestitures: $2.7 billion pre-tax (and after tax) in Q3 2022 from the split-off and combination of Food Safety with Neogen Corporation.
- Goodwill impairment: charge in Advanced Materials (within Transportation and Electronics) tied to decision to exit PFAS manufacturing.
- Other expense (income), net:
  - Net interest expense decreased in 2022 due to debt maturities and higher interest income; 2021 decrease reflected 2020 early debt extinguishment savings.
  - Non-service pension/postretirement net benefit: decreased $49 million in 2022; increased $163 million in 2021, driven by higher discount rates, lower expected asset returns, and changes in actuarial loss amortization.
- Provision for income taxes:
  - Effective tax rate: 9.6% in 2022 vs. 17.8% in 2021
  - Variability due to discrete items and geographic income mix
- Income from unconsolidated subsidiaries (equity method): $11 million in 2022 vs. $10 million in 2021; sale of remaining Kindeva interest in Q4 2022 with immaterial gain.
- Net income attributable to noncontrolling interest: $14 million in 2022 vs. $8 million in 2021; primarily related to 3M India Limited (75% owned).
- Performance by business segment:
  - Update in Q1 2022 to the measure of segment operating performance (business segment operating income) to align with CODM’s assessment and resource allocation.
  - 3M operates in four reportable segments: Safety and Industrial; Transportation and Electronics; Health Care; Consumer.

structure.heading: Performance by Business Segment
structure.start_phrase: Item 1, Business Segments, provides an overview of 3M’s business segments.
structure.summary:
- Covers financial line items and segment performance for 3M, with cross-references to Notes for details (Notes 2, 3, 5, 6, 10, 13, 15, 16, 19).
- Other expense (income), net: Interest expense (net) decreased in 2022 and 2021 due to debt maturities and higher interest income (2022) and 2020 early debt extinguishment savings (2021). Non-service pension/postretirement benefit decreased $49 million in 2022 and increased $163 million in 2021; 2022 change driven by higher discount-rate interest costs, lower expected asset returns, partly offset by lower actuarial loss amortization.
- Provision for income taxes: Effective tax rate was 9.6% in 2022 vs 17.8% in 2021. Variability driven by discrete items (audit settlements, tax law changes, share-based accounting) and recurring factors (geographic mix).
- Income from unconsolidated subsidiaries: $11 million in 2022 vs $10 million in 2021, primarily equity-method earnings (e.g., Kindeva); 3M sold its remaining Kindeva stake in Q4 2022 with an immaterial gain.
- Net income attributable to noncontrolling interest: $14 million in 2022 vs $8 million in 2021, mainly from 3M India Limited (3M owns 75%).
- Segment reporting: CODM performance measure changed in Q1 2022; business segment operating income updated for all periods. Four reportable segments: Safety & Industrial; Transportation & Electronics; Health Care; Consumer.
- Corporate and Unallocated: Includes corporate special items (major litigation for Combat Arms Earplugs and respirator/asbestos matters during Aearo’s chapter 11 period beginning July 2022; PFAS-related environmental matters; divestiture gains/costs; divestiture-related restructuring; Russia exit costs) and other corporate expense-net (unallocated staff/centers, philanthropy, transition services with Neogen and the Drug Delivery buyer). Corporate special item net costs decreased in 2022 due to the Food Safety split-off gain, partly offset by additional PFAS commitments (e.g., Zwijndrecht). Other corporate expense-net rose vs 2021 which had a $91 million benefit from a favorable Brazilian Supreme Court ruling on social taxes.
- Use of non-GAAP measures: Segment operating income is shown both as reported and adjusted for special items.
- Safety & Industrial (33.9% of sales): 2022 sales down 3.2% (organic +1.0%; translation –4.2%). Organic growth in electrical markets, abrasives, auto aftermarket, roofing granules, closure/masking, industrial adhesives/tapes; decline in personal safety from disposable respirator normalization (–4.5 pp to organic growth). Operating margin fell due to a ~$1.2 billion litigation charge and cost inflation/productivity headwinds; adjusted margin down slightly. 2021 grew 9.2% with margin pressure from inflation and litigation.
- Transportation & Electronics (26.0%): 2022 sales down 3.9% (organic +1.2%; divestitures –0.5%; translation –4.6%). Growth in automotive/aerospace, commercial solutions, advanced materials; declines in transportation safety and electronics due to weak consumer electronics and semiconductor constraints; Aearo deconsolidation reduced sales. Margin down from ~$0.8 billion PFAS manufacturing exit asset impairments, inflation, Belgium operational shutdown, and EV investments; adjusted margin up. 2021 up 10.2% with leverage benefits partly offset by inflation.
- Health Care (24.6%): 2022 sales down 2.0% (organic +3.2%; divestitures –1.4%; translation –3.8%). Growth in separation & purification, health information systems, food safety (pre-split-off), medical solutions; flat oral care; elective procedure and inflation headwinds. Margin down from inflation, productivity headwinds, investments, and Food Safety transaction costs. 3M announced a Health Care spin-off, expecting to retain 19.9%. 2021 up 9.8% with leverage and restructuring benefits.
- Consumer (15.5%): 2022 sales down 3.9% (organic –0.9%; divestitures –0.4%; translation –2.6%). Strength in stationery/office and home care; flat consumer health & safety; weakness in home improvement. Demand softened as consumers cut discretionary spend and retailers reduced inventories; demand remained for ScotchBlue painter’s tape, Scotch-Brite, and Post-it solutions. Margin down due to inflation, outsourced manufacturing, and productivity headwinds. 2021 up 10.8%.
- Geographic performance: Geographic data used as a secondary measure; sales recorded where final customer sales occur and may not reflect end-user consumption due to customer export activity; additional details in Notes 2 and 19.

structure.title: Performance by Geographic Area
structure.heading: Performance by Geographic Area
structure.start_phrase:
While 3M manages its businesses globally and believes its business segment results are the most relevant measure of performance, the Company also utilizes geographic area
data as a secondary performance measure.
structure.summary:
- Focuses on 3M’s Consumer Business segment (15.5% of consolidated sales), detailing 2022 and 2021 performance.
- 2022 Consumer results: sales $5.30B, down 3.9% in U.S. dollars; sales change drivers were organic -0.9%, divestitures -0.4%, currency translation -2.6%. Organic trends: growth in stationery/office and home care, flat in consumer health and safety, decline in home improvement. Demand pressures from consumers cutting discretionary spend and retailers reducing inventories, partially offset by strength in ScotchBlue painter’s tape, Scotch-Brite, and Post-it products. Operating income $994M; margin 18.8%, down due to higher raw materials, logistics, outsourced manufacturing costs, productivity headwinds, and investments, partially offset by pricing, spending discipline, and restructuring.
- 2021 Consumer results: sales $5.51B, up 10.8% in U.S. dollars; sales change drivers were organic +9.8% and currency translation +1.0%. Broad-based organic growth across categories, driven by strong demand for Command adhesives, Filtrete air quality solutions, Meguiar’s auto care, ScotchBlue painter’s tape, packaging/shipping products, Post-it solutions, and Scotch brand office tapes. Operating margin declined year over year due to higher input/logistics costs, productivity impacts, and increased compensation/benefits despite sales leverage and restructuring benefits.
- Explains 3M’s approach to geographic performance: business is managed globally with geographic data as a secondary measure; export sales are reported where final sales occur; regional net sales are not a proxy for end-user consumption. References Notes 2 and 19 and the Overview section for regional sales summaries.
- Geographic supplemental data (2022 vs. 2021): employment decreased to 92,000 from 95,000 (Americas 54k, Asia Pacific 18k, EMEA 20k). Capital spending rose to $1.75B from $1.60B (Americas $1.32B, Asia Pacific $182M, EMEA $246M). Net property, plant and equipment decreased to $9.18B from $9.43B (Americas $6.07B, Asia Pacific $1.39B, EMEA $1.72B). Notes continued investment to align manufacturing/sourcing with regional demand, emphasizing automation, efficiency, safety, and sustainability.
- Introduces critical accounting estimates, highlighting uncertainty and Audit Committee oversight. Key areas: legal proceedings (liabilities accrued when probable and reasonably estimable per ASC 450; see Note 16) and pension/postretirement obligations (key assumptions include discount rates and expected return on assets; see Note 13).

structure.title: Critical Accounting Estimates
structure.heading: Critical Accounting Estimates
structure.start_phrase: Information regarding significant accounting policies is included in Note 1 to the consolidated financial statements.
structure.summary:
- Geographic area supplemental data:
  - Employees, capital spending, and net property, plant and equipment (PP&E) reported by region (Americas; Asia Pacific; Europe, Middle East and Africa) for 2022 and 2021.
  - Company totals: employees decreased to 92,000 in 2022 from 95,000 in 2021; capital spending rose to $1.749 billion from $1.603 billion; net PP&E was $9.178 billion versus $9.429 billion.
  - Notes that employment changes reflect acquisitions, divestitures, and other actions.
  - Capital investments focus on capacity, regional alignment, efficiency, automation, safety, and sustainability; additional discussion referenced in MD&A under Cash Flows from Investing Activities.
- Critical accounting estimates:
  - Legal proceedings: accruals for probable and reasonably estimable claims under ASC 450; process details referenced in Note 16.
  - Pension and postretirement obligations:
    - Discount rate methodology uses a spot yield curve matched to projected cash flows; 2022 liability discount rates noted for major plans (e.g., U.S. qualified pension ~5.18%).
    - Expected return on assets assumptions increased for 2023 (U.S. plan 7.50% vs. 6.00% in 2022; international weighted average 4.61% vs. 3.86%).
    - 2022 total defined benefit pre-tax expense was $178 million; 2023 expected to decrease to about $145 million (service cost ~ $270 million; non-service benefit ~ $125 million).
  - Goodwill:
    - Goodwill totaled about $12.8 billion at 12/31/22.
    - Annual impairment testing (as of Oct 1, 2022) indicated no impairment; however, the December 2022 plan to exit PFAS manufacturing triggered additional testing and a goodwill impairment in the Advanced Materials reporting unit.
    - Ten primary reporting units account for ~94% of goodwill (including divisions such as Advanced Materials, Display Materials and Systems, Electronics Materials Solutions, Health Information Systems, Industrial Adhesives and Tapes, Medical Solutions, Oral Care, Personal Safety, Separation and Purification Sciences, Transportation Safety).
  - Long-lived assets:
    - Impairment recorded in December 2022 due to the PFAS exit decision; fair values primarily determined via discounted cash flow models using assumptions for sales, EBITDA margins, capital expenditures, and discount rates; significant uncertainties acknowledged.
  - Uncertain tax positions:
    - Reserves recorded under ASC 740 across multiple jurisdictions; outcomes may differ materially from estimates; liabilities adjusted as facts change.
- New accounting pronouncements: referenced in Note 1 to the consolidated financial statements.

structure.title: New Accounting Pronouncements
structure.heading: New Accounting Pronouncements
structure.start_phrase: Information regarding new accounting pronouncements is included in Note 1 to the Consolidated Financial Statements.
structure.summary:
- Goodwill impairment testing is conducted at the reporting unit (division) level using primarily a market approach (EBITDA multiples) and, where warranted, discounted cash flow analyses with assumptions for sales, EBITDA margins, capital expenditures, and discount rates; estimates are subject to market and economic uncertainties.
- In the annual test as of October 1, 2022, no goodwill impairment was indicated across 21 reporting units; roughly 94% of goodwill resided in ten divisions: Advanced Materials; Display Materials and Systems; Electronics Materials Solutions; Health Information Systems; Industrial Adhesives and Tapes; Medical Solutions; Oral Care; Personal Safety; Separation and Purification Sciences; Transportation Safety.
- Following 3M’s December 2022 decision to exit PFAS manufacturing, the Advanced Materials and Electronics Materials Solutions reporting units were retested, resulting in a goodwill impairment charge for Advanced Materials; ongoing monitoring for 2023 is planned.
- Long-lived assets are tested for impairment upon triggering events by comparing carrying value to undiscounted cash flows; any impairment is measured against fair value, primarily via DCF models using assumptions similar to goodwill testing. The PFAS exit led to a December 2022 impairment charge for certain long-lived assets, with significant estimation uncertainty cited.
- Uncertain income tax positions are recognized under ASC 740 based on expected audit outcomes across jurisdictions; reserves are adjusted as facts evolve, with potential for material charges or benefits upon resolution (see Note 10).
- New accounting pronouncements are discussed in Note 1.
- Financial condition and liquidity: strong free cash flow and market access support capital deployment priorities—investing in R&D, capex, and commercialization; active portfolio management (M&A/divestitures); and returning cash via dividends and share repurchases.
- U.S. cash needs are funded by domestic operations, capital market access, and repatriation of foreign earnings not permanently reinvested; indefinitely reinvested foreign earnings are not planned for repatriation (see Note 10).
- Liquidity: primary short-term needs covered by cash and a U.S. commercial paper program (up to $5 billion, maturities up to 397 days); no commercial paper outstanding at year-end 2022 or 2021.
- Debt profile: strong credit metrics with staggered maturities; ratings of A1 (stable) from Moody’s and A+ (CreditWatch negative) from S&P as of December 2022. Total debt declined in 2022 due to repayments of €500 million and $600 million medium-term notes.
- LIBOR transition: contracts referencing LIBOR are being modified as USD LIBOR publication ends June 30, 2023.
- Capital markets programs: WKSI shelf updated February 10, 2020; medium-term notes (Series F) capacity up to $18 billion, with approximately $17.6 billion issued as of December 31, 2022 (including prior years and FX effects).
- Food Safety Division split-off/Neogen combination financing: $1.0 billion in term loan and bridge commitments (bridge unused and terminated) and a $150 million revolving facility; upon the September 2022 split-off, term loan proceeds funded a cash payment to 3M, and related obligations transferred to Neogen.

structure.title: Financial Condition and Liquidity
structure.heading: Financial Condition and Liquidity
structure.start_phrase:
The strength and stability of 3M’s business model and strong free cash flow capability, together with proven capital markets access, provide financial flexibility to deploy
capital in accordance with the Company's stated priorities and meet needs associated with contractual commitments and other obligations.
structure.summary:
- Focus on financial condition, liquidity, and capital allocation: prioritize organic investment (R&D, capex, commercialization), active portfolio management (acquisitions/divestitures), and returning cash via dividends and share repurchases. U.S. cash needs met through domestic cash flows, capital markets, and selective repatriation; certain foreign earnings remain indefinitely reinvested.

- Liquidity and short-term funding: strong profile with primary reliance on cash and a $5 billion U.S. commercial paper program (max 397-day maturity); no commercial paper outstanding at 12/31/22 or 12/31/21.

- Debt and credit profile: staggered maturities; Moody’s A1 (stable) and S&P A+ (CreditWatch negative). Total debt decreased to $15.9B at 12/31/22 from $17.4B at 12/31/21, driven by repayments of €500M (Feb 2022) and $600M (Jun 2022) notes. LIBOR transition underway. WKSI shelf in place; Series F MTN capacity $18B with ~$17.6B issued by 12/31/22. Food Safety split-off financing facilities ($1.0B term/bridge and $150M revolver) established; bridge unused and all obligations transferred to Neogen at closing.

- Cash, cash equivalents, and marketable securities: $3.9B at 12/31/22 ($2.7B foreign, $1.2B U.S.) vs $4.8B at 12/31/21; decline reflects operating cash flows, Food Safety transaction cash logistics and earlier borrowings offset by dividends, buybacks, capex, and 2022 note maturities.

- Net debt (non-GAAP): $12.0B at 12/31/22 vs $12.6B at 12/31/21.

- Balance sheet and working capital (non-GAAP): working capital declined to $5.2B from $6.4B, driven by lower cash and higher short-term borrowings/current portion of LT debt, partially offset by lower accrued payroll. Inventory up $387M on higher activity (partly offset by FX); accounts payable higher.

- Cash flows:
  - Operating activities: $5.6B in 2022 vs $7.5B in 2021; decline due to lower net income and U.S. tax capitalization of R&D; working capital reduced cash flow; included ~$1.2B pre-tax charge related to Combat Arms Earplugs litigation; non-cash impairments tied to PFAS exit added back.
  - Investing activities: $(1.0)B in 2022 vs $(1.3)B in 2021; capex $1.75B; $478M cash received from Food Safety split-off; continued investment in growth, productivity, IT, labs, sustainability. 2023 capex expected at $1.5–$1.8B. Active management of marketable securities portfolio.
  - Financing activities: $(5.35)B in 2022 vs $(6.15)B in 2021; net debt reduction $(0.84)B; share repurchases $1.46B; dividends $3.37B; no CP outstanding year-end. Non-cash debt-for-debt exchange in Food Safety split-off reduced $350M of 3M CP and became Neogen term debt.

- Shareholder returns: $1.464B of share repurchases in 2022; no equity-linked derivatives used. Dividends increased to $1.50 per share in Feb 2023 (annual $6.00), marking 65 consecutive years of increases.

- Free cash flow (non-GAAP): $3.842B in 2022 vs $5.851B in 2021; free cash flow conversion 66% vs 99%.

- Material cash requirements: obligations related to taxes, debt (including approximately $6B future interest), commitments/contingencies, and leases. Limited unconditional purchase obligations and small contractual capital commitments.

- Financial instruments and market risk:
  - Governance and counterparty risk: senior management oversight of risk policies; use of major international banks; exposure limited to instrument fair values; no anticipated counterparty nonperformance.
  - Foreign exchange risk: use of forwards/options as cash flow hedges (hedge horizon up to 36 months) and undesignated hedges for non-functional currency items; net investment hedges via forwards and foreign-currency debt. Notional amounts at 12/31/22: $3.2B designated FX hedges; $2.8B undesignated; €2.4B debt designated as net investment hedge.
  - Interest rate risk: mix of fixed/floating debt; use of fair value interest rate swaps ($800M notional at 12/31/22).
  - Commodity risk: managed via negotiated supply contracts and price protection agreements.

structure.title: Financial Instruments
structure.heading: Financial Instruments
structure.start_phrase: The Company enters into foreign exchange forward contracts, options and swaps to hedge against the effect of exchange rate fluctuations on cash flows denominated in foreign currencies and to offset, in part, the impacts of changes in value of various non-functional currency denominated items including certain intercompany financing balances.
structure.summary:
- Focuses on 3M’s use of financial instruments to manage market risks—foreign exchange, interest rates, and commodity prices—within Item 7A (Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures About Market Risk).
- Describes governance: senior management oversees risk policies, derivative utilization, controls, valuation, risk analysis, counterparty approval, and ongoing monitoring/reporting.
- Addresses counterparty credit risk: exposure limited to instrument fair value; risk managed via credit approvals/limits and use of major international banks; no anticipated nonperformance.
- Foreign exchange risk: exposure from net investments, cash flows, and translation of earnings. Use of FX forwards and options as cash flow hedges (hedge horizon up to 36 months; may de-designate before forecasted transactions occur) and non-designated FX contracts to offset remeasurement of non-functional currency items (including intercompany balances). Also uses FX forwards and foreign-currency debt for net investment hedges.
- Interest rate risk: managed through a mix of fixed and floating rate debt and interest rate swaps designated as fair value hedges.
- Commodity price risk: managed through negotiated supply contracts and price protection agreements.
- Notional amounts at December 31, 2022: $3.2 billion of FX forwards/options designated as cash flow or net investment hedges; $2.8 billion of FX contracts not designated as hedges; €2.4 billion of foreign currency–denominated debt designated as non-derivative net investment hedges; $800 million of interest rate swaps.
- Cross-references to Item 7A for market risk and VaR discussion, Note 12 for long-term debt, and Note 14 for derivative and hedging details.

structure.title: Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures About Market Risk
structure.heading: ITEM 7A Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures About Market Risk
structure.start_phrase:
In the context of Item 7A, 3M is exposed to market risk due to the risk of loss arising from adverse changes in foreign currency exchange rates, interest rates and commodity
prices.
structure.summary:
- Focus: 3M’s Item 7A Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures About Market Risk and related Financial Instruments.
- Risk areas covered: foreign currency exchange, interest rates, and commodity prices; includes governance, hedging strategies, counterparty credit risk, and value-at-risk (VaR) analysis.
- Governance/controls: Senior management oversees risk policies, derivative use, controls, valuation, risk analysis, counterparty approvals, and ongoing monitoring/reporting. Credit exposure is limited to derivative fair values; counterparties are major global banks with monitored limits.
- Foreign exchange risk management:
  - Uses forward and option contracts as cash flow hedges (hedge horizon up to 36 months) and nondesignated hedges for non-functional currency items (including intercompany balances).
  - Employs foreign currency forward contracts and foreign-currency-denominated debt as net investment hedges.
  - Notional amounts at 12/31/22: $3.2B (designated FX hedges), $2.8B (nondesignated FX), plus €2.4B of FX debt designated as non-derivative net investment hedges.
- Interest rate risk management:
  - Mix of fixed and floating rate debt; may use interest rate swaps designated as fair value hedges.
  - Notional amount of interest rate swaps at 12/31/22: $800M.
- Commodity price risk management: Addressed via negotiated supply contracts and price protection agreements.
- Value-at-Risk (VaR) analysis:
  - Annual Monte Carlo simulation (third-party dataset), 95% confidence over a 12-month horizon; assesses after-tax earnings sensitivity to currency, interest rate, and commodity exposures outstanding at 12/31/22.
  - 2022 modeled impacts on after-tax earnings: FX adverse $(315)M/positive $314M; interest adverse $(18)M/positive $18M; commodities adverse $(5)M/positive $7M. Comparable 2021 figures provided (smaller FX and interest impacts; larger adverse commodity impact).
- Additional sensitivity:
  - 1% change in purchased components/materials ≈ $85M annual pre-tax impact.
  - 10% change in global energy prices ≈ $45M annual pre-tax impact (electricity and natural gas).
- Cross-references: Note 12 (long-term debt), Note 14 (derivatives/hedging, including net investment hedges), and Item 8 (Financial Statements and auditor report, PCAOB ID 238).

structure.title: Financial Statements and Supplementary Data
structure.heading: ITEM 8 Financial Statements and Supplementary Data
structure.start_phrase: A complete summary of Form 10-K content, including the index to financial statements, is found at the beginning of this document.
structure.summary:
- Presents a Value at Risk (VaR) analysis performed annually to assess 3M’s sensitivity to foreign exchange rates, interest rates, and commodity prices.
- Describes methodology: Monte Carlo simulation using a third-party bank dataset, 95% confidence level, 12-month horizon, based on exposures outstanding at December 31, 2022; includes a disclaimer that model results may not reflect actual outcomes.
- Summarizes potential after-tax earnings impacts (in millions):
  - Foreign exchange: 2022 adverse (315), positive 314; 2021 adverse (140), positive 147.
  - Interest rates: 2022 adverse (18), positive 18; 2021 adverse (2), positive 2.
  - Commodity prices: 2022 adverse (5), positive 7; 2021 adverse (21), positive 14.
- Notes procurement and energy sensitivity:
  - A 1% change in purchased components/materials prices would impact pre-tax costs/savings by approximately $85 million per year.
  - A 10% change in global energy prices (electricity and natural gas used in 3M facilities) would impact pre-tax costs/savings by approximately $45 million per year.
- Introduces Item 8: Financial Statements and Supplementary Data, including the Report of Independent Registered Public Accounting Firm (PCAOB ID 238), Consolidated Financial Statements, and the Index to Financial Statements, with a reference to the complete Form 10-K summary and index at the beginning of the document.

structure.title: Index to Financial Statements
structure.heading: Index to Financial Statements
structure.start_phrase: A complete summary of Form 10-K content, including the index to financial statements, is found at the beginning of this document.
structure.summary:
- Annual Value at Risk analysis assessing sensitivity to foreign exchange, interest rates, and commodity prices using a Monte Carlo simulation (95% confidence, 12-month horizon, third‑party bank dataset) on exposures outstanding at December 31, 2022; includes a table of potential adverse and positive after-tax earnings impacts for 2022 and 2021:
  - Foreign exchange: 2022 adverse $(315)M / positive $314M; 2021 adverse $(140)M / positive $147M
  - Interest rates: 2022 adverse $(18)M / positive $18M; 2021 adverse $(2)M / positive $2M
  - Commodity prices: 2022 adverse $(5)M / positive $7M; 2021 adverse $(21)M / positive $14M
  - Model is sensitivity-focused and not predictive.
- Additional exposure analyses:
  - Purchased components/materials: a 1% price change ≈ $85M annual pre-tax cost or savings.
  - Global energy (electricity and natural gas): a 10% price change ≈ $45M annual pre-tax cost or savings.
- Item 8: Financial Statements and Supplementary Data, including Report of Independent Registered Public Accounting Firm (PCAOB ID 238), Consolidated Financial Statements, and index reference.
- Management’s Responsibility for Financial Reporting: preparation under U.S. GAAP, use of estimates, maintenance of internal controls to safeguard assets and ensure accurate records and fair presentation; company-wide ethical policies; ongoing internal audit review.
- Management’s Report on Internal Control Over Financial Reporting: assessment under COSO 2013 concluding controls were effective as of December 31, 2022; PwC audited ICFR and issued an unqualified opinion as of that date.

structure.title: Management’s Responsibility for Financial Reporting
structure.heading: Management’s Responsibility for Financial Reporting
structure.start_phrase: Management is responsible for the integrity and objectivity of the financial information included in this report.
structure.summary:
- The document outlines 3M management’s responsibility for the integrity and objectivity of financial reporting and preparation of financial statements in accordance with U.S. GAAP, including the use of reasonable estimates.
- It describes the company’s system of internal control over financial reporting designed to safeguard assets, ensure accurate books and records, enforce policies by qualified personnel, and support fair presentation of published financial statements.
- It highlights company-wide written policies, including business conduct/ethics standards, and the ongoing review of controls by internal auditors.
- Management reports on its assessment of internal control over financial reporting using the COSO Internal Control — Integrated Framework (2013), concluding controls were effective as of December 31, 2022.
- An independent audit by PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP affirms this conclusion with an unqualified opinion on the effectiveness of 3M’s internal control over financial reporting as of December 31, 2022.

structure.title: Management’s Report on Internal Control Over Financial Reporting
structure.heading: Management’s Report on Internal Control Over Financial Reporting
structure.start_phrase: Management is responsible for establishing and maintaining an adequate system of internal control over financial reporting.
structure.summary:
- Management asserts responsibility for the integrity and objectivity of financial reporting, preparation of financial statements in accordance with U.S. GAAP, and use of estimates where needed.
- A system of internal control over financial reporting is maintained to safeguard assets, ensure accurate records, implement policies with qualified personnel, uphold high ethical standards through business conduct policies, and support fair presentation; internal auditors provide ongoing review.
- Management’s assessment of internal control over financial reporting, conducted using COSO’s Internal Control—Integrated Framework (2013), concluded controls were effective as of December 31, 2022.
- PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP (PwC), an independent registered public accounting firm, audited both the consolidated financial statements (for the three years ended December 31, 2022) and the effectiveness of internal control over financial reporting as of December 31, 2022.
- PwC issued unqualified opinions: the financial statements present fairly in conformity with U.S. GAAP and internal control over financial reporting was effective as of December 31, 2022.
- The auditor describes its responsibilities, independence, and procedures under PCAOB standards, including risk assessment, testing, and evaluation of accounting principles and significant estimates.
- The document explains the definition and inherent limitations of internal control over financial reporting, emphasizing reasonable (not absolute) assurance and potential changes over time that may affect effectiveness.

structure.title: Report of Independent Registered Public Accounting Firm
structure.heading: Report of Independent Registered Public Accounting Firm
structure.start_phrase:
We have audited the accompanying consolidated balance sheet of 3M Company and its subsidiaries (the “Company”) as of December 31, 2022 and 2021, and the related
consolidated statements of income, of comprehensive income (loss), of changes in equity and of cash flows for each of the three years in the period ended December 31, 2022,
including the related notes (collectively referred to as the “consolidated financial statements”).
structure.summary:
- Independent auditor’s report from PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP to 3M’s Board and shareholders covering:
  - Unqualified opinions that: (1) the consolidated financial statements present fairly, in all material respects, 3M’s financial position as of Dec 31, 2022 and 2021 and results/cash flows for each of the three years ended Dec 31, 2022 in conformity with U.S. GAAP; and (2) internal control over financial reporting (ICFR) was effective as of Dec 31, 2022 under COSO 2013.
  - Basis for opinions: management’s responsibilities, auditor independence and PCAOB standards, audit scope and procedures for both the financial statements and ICFR.
  - Definition and inherent limitations of ICFR.

- Critical Audit Matters (CAMs) and related audit procedures:
  - Legal proceedings: significant management judgment in assessing probability and estimating losses/ranges; auditor procedures included testing controls, legal inquiry letters, contract reviews, evaluating assessments and disclosures.
  - Tax-free determination of the Food Safety Division split-off (Reverse Morris Trust): significant judgment applying U.S. federal tax law; reliance on IRS private letter ruling, third-party tax opinions, and external advice; auditors used tax specialists and tested related controls and evidence supporting tax-free treatment.
  - Impairment assessments for Advanced Materials Division (property, plant & equipment and goodwill): triggered by 3M’s decision to exit PFAS manufacturing by end of 2025; 2022 pre-tax charge of ~$0.8B ($0.5B long-lived assets, $0.3B goodwill); fair values based on discounted cash flow models with key assumptions (projected sales, EBITDA margins, capex, discount rate); auditors tested controls, models, and assumptions, using specialists.

- Auditor details: PwC, Minneapolis, report dated February 8, 2023; auditor of 3M since 1975.

- Consolidated Statement of Income (Years ended Dec 31, 2022, 2021, 2020):
  - Net sales: $34,229M (2022), $35,355M (2021), $32,184M (2020).
  - Operating expenses include: cost of sales, SG&A ($9,049M in 2022 vs $7,197M in 2021), R&D ($1,862M in 2022), gain on business divestitures (2022: $(2,724)M), goodwill impairment ($271M in 2022).
  - Operating income: $6,539M (2022) vs $7,369M (2021).
  - Other expense (income), net: $147M (2022).
  - Provision for income taxes: $612M (2022) vs $1,285M (2021).
  - Net income attributable to 3M: $5,777M (2022), $5,921M (2021), $5,449M (2020).
  - EPS: Basic $10.21 and diluted $10.18 (2022); Basic $10.23 and diluted $10.12 (2021).
  - Shares outstanding (weighted average): Basic 566.0M (2022), Diluted 567.6M (2022).
  - Notes to the consolidated financial statements are integral to the statement.

structure.title: Consolidated Statement of Income for years ended December 31, 2022, 2021 and 2020
structure.heading: Consolidated Statement of Income for years ended December 31, 2022, 2021 and 2020
structure.start_phrase: The accompanying Notes to Consolidated Financial Statements are an integral part of this statement.
structure.summary:
- Presents 3M Company’s Consolidated Statements of Income and Comprehensive Income for the years ended December 31, 2022, 2021, and 2020.
- Income statement highlights:
  - Net sales: $34.2B (2022), down from $35.4B (2021), up from $32.2B (2020).
  - Operating expenses detail: cost of sales, SG&A (notably higher in 2022), R&D (slightly lower in 2022), a large gain on business divestitures in 2022 (-$2.7B) and 2020 (-$0.4B), and a 2022 goodwill impairment ($271M).
  - Operating income declined to $6.5B (2022) from $7.4B (2021).

structure.title: Notes to Consolidated Financial Statements
structure.heading: Notes to Consolidated Financial Statements
structure.start_phrase: 3M is a diversified global manufacturer, technology innovator and marketer of a wide variety of products.
structure.summary:
- Document section: 3M Company Notes to Consolidated Financial Statements, Note 1 – Significant Accounting Policies.
- Consolidation: 3M consolidates all applicable subsidiaries and eliminates intercompany transactions; deconsolidated the Aearo Entities in Q3 2022 (see Note 16).
- Basis of presentation: Prior-period reclassifications to conform to current presentation. In Q1 2022, 3M changed the measure of segment operating performance, affecting reported segment profit/loss and disaggregated revenue; all periods reflect these changes (see Notes 19 and 2).
- Foreign currency: Local currencies are generally the functional currency; exceptions for highly inflationary economies (Argentina and, beginning Q2 2022, Turkey). These subsidiaries are remeasured into the parent’s currency. Assets/liabilities translated at month-end rates; income/expenses at average monthly rates. Cumulative translation adjustments recorded in accumulated other comprehensive income (AOCI).
- Use of estimates: Preparation under U.S. GAAP requires estimates and assumptions; COVID-19 impacts considered and may change future estimates.
- Cash and cash equivalents: Cash and investments with original maturities of three months or less.
- Marketable securities: Available-for-sale debt securities at fair value; FIFO for cost of securities sold. Classified as current or non-current based on availability for operations. Impairment evaluated under ASC 320 and ASC 326-30: credit-related losses recognized via an allowance (limited to fair value shortfall) through earnings; non-credit impairments recorded in AOCI. Changes reclassified from AOCI to earnings upon sale or changes in credit/non-credit components.
- Investments: Equity securities not consolidated or equity-method are measured at fair value with changes in net income. For equity investments without readily determinable fair values, 3M uses the measurement alternative (cost minus impairment plus/minus observable price changes). Balance details in Note 7.

structure.title: Significant Accounting Policies
structure.heading: Note 1. Significant Accounting Policies
structure.start_phrase: 3M is a diversified global manufacturer, technology innovator and marketer of a wide variety of products.
structure.summary:
- Context: Notes to Consolidated Financial Statements for 3M Company, primarily Note 1 (Significant Accounting Policies) and portions of Note 2 (Revenue).
- Consolidation and presentation:
  - All applicable subsidiaries consolidated; intercompany transactions eliminated.
  - Aearo Entities deconsolidated in Q3 2022 (see Note 16).
  - Prior-period reclassifications to conform to current presentation.
  - 2022 changes to segment performance measures and disaggregated revenue (see Notes 19 and 2).
- Foreign currency:
  - Local currency generally functional; Argentina and, beginning Q2 2022, Turkey treated as highly inflationary with remeasurement to parent currency.
  - Translation methodology and AOCI treatment described.
- Use of estimates:
  - Estimates under U.S. GAAP with consideration of COVID-19-related uncertainties.
- Cash, investments, and marketable securities:
  - Cash equivalents = ≤3-month maturities.
  - Marketable securities classified as available-for-sale at fair value; FIFO for cost; credit loss model under ASC 320/326-30.
  - Equity investments at fair value or measurement alternative for non-marketable holdings (see Note 7).
- Other assets:
  - Include deferred taxes, product/insurance receivables, life insurance cash surrender value, medical equipment in rental arrangements, and pension-related items; cash flow presentation of life insurance activity specified.
- Inventories:
  - Lower of cost or NRV; generally FIFO.
- Property, plant and equipment:
  - Capitalization policies (including capitalized interest/internal engineering); straight-line depreciation with typical useful life ranges for buildings (10–40 years) and equipment (3–15 years).
  - Impairment triggers and fair value measurement; treatment of capital-related government grants.
- Asset retirement obligations:
  - Recognition, accretion, and depreciation policies; liability of approximately $177 million at 12/31/22.
- Goodwill and intangibles:
  - Goodwill not amortized; annual Q4 impairment testing at reporting-unit level using market or DCF approaches; Step 0 not elected.
  - Definite-lived intangibles (customer, patents, technology, tradenames) amortized over typical ranges (6–20 years) with impairment testing; indefinite-lived tradenames tested annually in Q3.
- Restructuring:
  - Accounting for severance, contract termination, and asset impairments; timing of recognition and measurement.
- Revenue recognition (ASC 606):
  - Predominantly single performance obligation to transfer goods; some arrangements include IP out-licensing, software with support, services, and multiple elements.
  - Control transfers mainly point-in-time; some over time.
  - Transaction price includes variable consideration (rebates, promotions, discounts) estimated using portfolio and most-likely-amount methods; returns and warranties addressed; sales taxes excluded from revenue.
  - Allocation to multiple performance obligations based on standalone selling prices.
  - No material remaining performance obligations >1 year; no material contract acquisition costs with amortization >1 year.
  - Practical expedients/exemptions used: short-term remaining obligations disclosure, expensing sales commissions, portfolio approach, right-to-invoice, net presentation for sales taxes, sales-based royalty exemption.
- Lease revenue (ASC 842):
  - Rental revenue recognition for short-term operating leases of durable medical devices based on usage; separate from ASC 606.
- Receivables and allowances:
  - Non-interest-bearing trade receivables; allowance methodology based on expected credit losses and historical discounts; long-term receivables with low credit risk; bad debt amounts not material.
- Operating expenses and R&D:
  - Advertising and merchandising expensed as incurred; totals disclosed for 2020–2022.
  - Research, development and related expenses presented separately; totals and components (basic research, patent costs, amortization of acquired IP, venture-related gains/losses) disclosed for 2020–2022.
- Internal-use software:
  - Capitalization of direct/internal costs; amortization over 3–7 years; presented in PP&E; removal upon full depreciation.
- Environmental:
  - Expense for past-condition remediation; capitalize qualifying projects; recognition of remediation reserves when probable and estimable.
- Income taxes (ASC 740):
  - Asset/liability approach for deferred taxes; valuation allowances disclosed; policy on uncertain tax positions.
- Earnings per share:
  - Basic and diluted EPS computations and share counts disclosed; anti-dilutive option counts noted.
- Stock-based compensation:
  - Programs (options, RSUs, performance shares, employee stock purchase); grant-date fair value expensing; tax effects (excess benefits/deficiencies) recognized in income tax expense and operating cash flows.
- Comprehensive income and AOCI:
  - Components include FX translation (including net investment hedges), pension/postretirement adjustments, AFS debt securities, and cash flow hedges; portfolio approach for releasing tax effects.
- Derivatives and hedging (ASC 815):
  - Use of interest rate swaps, currency swaps, and FX forwards/options; hedge accounting where applicable; undesignated instruments marked to market; cash flow classification aligned with hedged items; no trading or leveraged derivatives.
- Credit risk:
  - Counterparty risk management and master netting arrangements; gross presentation of derivative assets/liabilities elected.
- Fair value measurements (ASC 820):
  - Definition of fair value and three-level hierarchy; categorization principles.
- Acquisitions (ASC 805):
  - Recognition/measurement at acquisition-date fair value; treatment of contingent consideration and exclusion of transaction/restructuring costs; accounting for asset purchases/investments that are not business combinations.
- Leases (lessee accounting):
  - Identification of leases vs. service contracts; recognition of ROU assets and liabilities using incremental borrowing rate; leased asset types; CPI-based adjustments; renewal/termination option assessments; grouping lease and non-lease components; variable payment types.
- Related parties:
  - No material related party activity other than amounts between Aearo Entities and related entities (see Note 16).
- New accounting pronouncements:
  - ASU 2021-08 (Topic 805) on recognizing contract assets/liabilities in business combinations effective 1/1/2023.
  - ASU 2022-04 (Subtopic 405-50) on supplier finance program disclosures effective 1/1/2023; rollforward required for 2024 year-end; disclosure-only impact.
- Note 2 Revenue highlights:
  - Contract balances: deferred revenue primarily from one-year software licenses; significant portions of prior-year balances recognized in the following year.
  - Operating lease revenue: rental income from durable medical devices within Medical Solutions Division disclosed for 2020–2022.

- Scope: Excerpts from 3M’s Notes to Consolidated Financial Statements covering new accounting pronouncements, revenue recognition (including contract balances, operating lease revenue, and disaggregated sales), and acquisitions/divestitures.

- Presentation note: Gains/losses on business divestitures are reported in Corporate and Unallocated.

structure.title: Acquisitions and Divestitures
structure.heading: Note 3. Acquisitions and Divestitures
structure.start_phrase:
3M makes acquisitions of certain businesses from time to time that are aligned with its strategic intent with respect to, among other factors, growth markets and adjacent
product lines or technologies.
structure.summary:
- Note 3: Acquisitions and Divestitures
  - Strategy: 3M acquires and divests to align with growth markets, adjacent technologies, and capital deployment; divestiture gains/losses reported in Corporate and Unallocated.
  - Acquisitions: No acquisitions closed in 2020, 2021, or 2022.
  - 2022 divestitures and actions:
    - Sold Western Europe floor products business (Consumer) for immaterial proceeds.
    - Announced intention to spin off the Health Care business as a separate public company by year-end 2023; 3M to initially retain 19.9% ownership; intended to be tax-free for U.S. federal income tax purposes; subject to customary approvals and conditions; not classified as held for sale.
    - Completed split-off of Food Safety Division and combination with Neogen via Reverse Morris Trust:
      - Recognized $2.7 billion pre-tax gain on $2.8 billion aggregate consideration.
      - Consideration included: $2.0 billion value of 16 million 3M shares accepted in a fully-subscribed exchange offer (subscribing shareholders ended with 50.1% of Neogen) and $828 million funded from debt that became Neogen obligations ($478 million cash to 3M and $350 million non-cash debt-for-debt exchange reducing 3M commercial paper).
      - Tax treatment intended to be U.S. tax-free; 3M obtained IRS private letter ruling and third-party opinions; potential exposure if later determined non-qualifying.
      - Entered transition and longer-term supply/distribution agreements with Neogen; related sales info referenced in Note 2.
  - 2021 divestitures: None.
  - 2020 divestitures:
    - Sold advanced ballistic-protection business (Transportation & Electronics) to Avon Rubber for $86 million cash plus contingent consideration (potential additional < $25 million); business had ~$85 million annual sales; immaterial measurement and completion impacts.
    - Sold substantially all Drug Delivery Division (Health Care) to an Altaris affiliate for $617 million (cash $487 million, $70 million interest-bearing security, $60 million for a 17% noncontrolling interest in Kindeva); recognized $387 million pre-tax gain; accounted for Kindeva under equity method; sold remaining Kindeva interest in Q4 2022 with immaterial gain; included transition/supply agreements.
    - Sold a small dermatology products business for immaterial proceeds approximating book value.
  - Operating income and held-for-sale: Health Care segment operating income (inclusive of Food Safety and Drug Delivery) referenced in Note 19; immaterial held-for-sale balances at Dec 31, 2021 and none at Dec 31, 2022; other held-for-sale groups in Note 15.

structure.summary:
- Note 4: Goodwill and Intangible Assets
  - No goodwill recognized from acquisitions in 2021 or 2022; changes largely reflect foreign currency translation.
  - Goodwill by segment declined from $13.8 billion at 12/31/2020 to $13.5 billion at 12/31/2021 and $12.8 billion at 12/31/2022.
  - 2022 activity: $16 million goodwill reduction from divestitures; $271 million goodwill impairment in the Advanced Materials reporting unit (Transportation & Electronics) tied to the PFAS exit, leaving no remaining goodwill in that unit. Annual Q4 2022 impairment testing otherwise indicated no impairment.
  - Reporting unit realignments in early 2022 (per Note 19) used the relative fair value method; goodwill reassignments were immaterial.
  - Finite-lived acquired intangibles at 12/31/2022: gross $7.8 billion, accumulated amortization $3.7 billion, net $4.1 billion; non-amortizable intangibles $0.6 billion; total intangibles net $4.7 billion (down from $5.3 billion in 2021).
  - Certain long-standing tradenames are indefinite-lived and not amortized.
  - PFAS exit (Note 15) also resulted in impairment of long-lived assets and an immaterial impairment to indefinite-lived intangibles in Q4 2022.
  - Amortization expense: $537 million (2020), $529 million (2021), $498 million (2022). Expected amortization (as of 12/31/2022): 2023 $479m, 2024 $451m, 2025 $421m, 2026 $415m, 2027 $390m, thereafter $1,926m; subject to change with acquisitions, FX, impairments, etc.

- Note 5: Restructuring Actions (2020–2022 Operational/Marketing Capability Initiative)
  - Program launched in late 2020 to streamline operations and marketing, shift toward faster-growing markets, and de-prioritize slower-growth areas.
  - Pre-tax charges: $137 million (2020), $124 million (2021), $18 million (Q1 2022); total about $280 million over the program.
  - Approximately 3,100 positions impacted worldwide.

- Note 5 – Restructuring actions:
  - 2020–2022 Operational/Marketing Capability Restructuring: Initiative launched in late 2020 and completed with actions committed in Q1 2022; impacted ~3,100 positions and generated total pre‑tax charges of ~$280 million ($137M in 2020, $124M in 2021, $18M in 2022). Charges were recorded across cost of sales, SG&A, and R&D, with detailed impacts by business segment. Cash and non‑cash roll‑forwards of restructuring accruals are provided; activities largely completed in Q3 2022.
  - 2022 Divestiture‑related Restructuring (post Food Safety split‑off/Neogen combination): Affected ~850 positions; Q3 2022 pre‑tax charge of $41 million in Corporate & Unallocated, recorded across cost of sales, SG&A, and R&D. Cash payments reduced the accrual to $10 million at year‑end 2022; expected completion largely by H1 2023.
  - 2020 Divestiture‑related Restructuring (post Drug Delivery divestiture): Affected ~1,300 positions; Q2 2020 pre‑tax charge of $55 million, with allocations across cost of sales, SG&A, and R&D. Includes cash/non‑cash movements and accrual roll‑forward; largely completed in Q3 2021.
  - 2020 Other Restructuring (COVID‑19 related): Addressed structural costs and operations in certain end markets; impacted ~400 positions; Q2 2020 pre‑tax charge of $58 million with segment and P&L line detail. Roll‑forward shows non‑cash impacts and cash payments; largely completed in Q2 2021.

For 2020–2022, interest expense declined year over year; interest income increased; pension/postretirement reflected net benefits in 2021 and 2022. - Note 12 details 3M’s long-term debt and short-term borrowings as of December 31, 2022 (with 2021 comparatives), showing for each instrument the currency, fixed vs. floating status, effective interest rate (post-swap), final maturity, and carrying value.

- Post-swap mix of long-term debt (including current portion): $14,738 million fixed-rate at a 2.93% effective rate and $1,201 million floating-rate at 5.70% (2021: $16,053 million fixed at 2.80% and $1,294 million floating at 1.43%).

- Credit facilities: an undrawn $3.0 billion five-year revolving credit facility expiring Nov 2024 (expandable by $1.0 billion) and an undrawn $1.25 billion 364‑day facility expiring Nov 2023 with a term-out option. Covenant requires EBITDA/Interest ≥ 3.0x; actual ~19x at year-end 2022; no dividend restrictions.
- Food Safety Division financing related to the Neogen split-off: $1.0 billion in term loan/bridge commitments and a $150 million revolver established in 2021/2022. Bridge was terminated unused; obligations transferred to Neogen at closing; term loans funded the cash payment to 3M.
- Other credit facilities: $318 million of stand-alone letters of credit and bank guarantees outstanding at year-end 2022.
- Swaps and issuances: In 2021, $800 million of interest rate swaps converted portions of 2049 and 2050 fixed notes ($500m and $300m, respectively) to floating through mid‑2028 (3‑month LIBOR based). In March 2020, 3M issued $1.75 billion of registered notes (2025 2.65%, 2030 3.05%, 2050 3.70%).
- Debt maturities/extinguishments: 2022 repayments included €500 million (Feb) and $600 million (Jun) fixed-rate notes. 2021 repayments included €600 million Eurobonds and a $450 million 2.75% 2022 note via make‑whole (resulting in an $11 million pre‑tax charge). 2020 repayments included $1.0 billion via make‑wholes (incurring a $10 million pre‑tax charge) and maturities of €650 million and $500 million floating-rate notes.
- Floating-rate notes carry put provisions allowing holders to require repurchase at specified percentages of par on scheduled dates; repurchases in the periods presented were immaterial. A $60 million 40‑year FRN due 2044 has an annual put feature since 2014; other FRNs have put options beginning 10 years post‑issuance and every third anniversary thereafter.
- Note 13 begins with an overview of pension and postretirement benefit plans: over 75 defined benefit plans across 28 countries; benefits based on service, compensation, and age. The primary U.S. defined benefit plan closed to new participants on Jan 1, 2009. Certain U.S. employees (employed before Jan 1, 2016) receive postretirement health and life benefits; international postretirement health costs are not material. Plan assets are held with independent trustees; the non‑qualified plan has no plan assets. For U.S. postretirement health and life plans, amounts at least equal to annual benefit payments are set aside with a trustee.
